2. People who already have heart problems are highly SUSCEPTIBLE to being badly affected by a bout of flu. --- SUSCEPTIBLE (adj) = dễ mắc, dễ bị ảnh hưởng; luôn đi với giới từ "to" (susceptible TO illness/infection), không dùng "with" hay "for".

3. Cutting down on salt and getting more sleep can gradually AMELIORATE high blood pressure. --- AMELIORATE (v, formal) = cải thiện một tình trạng vốn đã xấu; collocation "ameliorate symptoms/risk factors/a situation"; không dùng chung chung như "improve" (VD: không nói "ameliorate your English").

4. After breaking her hip, she spent three months undergoing REHABILITATION to relearn how to walk. --- REHABILITATION (n) = sự phục hồi chức năng sau chấn thương/bệnh tật; collocation "undergo rehabilitation", "a rehabilitation programme"; động từ liên quan "rehabilitate".

5. Better sanitation and access to clean water have quietly increased average human LONGEVITY. --- LONGEVITY (n, formal) = tuổi thọ, khái niệm trừu tượng về sự trường thọ; collocation "increased longevity", "human longevity"; phân biệt với "life expectancy" (chỉ số thống kê cụ thể).

6. Skipping breakfast every day and living on instant noodles is clearly DETRIMENTAL to a teenager's growth and concentration. --- DETRIMENTAL (adj, formal) = có hại, gây tổn hại; cấu trúc cố định "detrimental TO sth", không dùng "for"; trang trọng hơn "bad for".

7. A flu EPIDEMIC spread through three provinces last month, filling hospital wards within weeks. --- EPIDEMIC (n) = dịch bệnh lan rộng trong một khu vực/cộng đồng; collocation "a flu epidemic", "reach epidemic proportions"; khác "pandemic" (đại dịch lan ra toàn cầu).

8. Ignoring a mild cough for months can EXACERBATE a minor infection into a much more serious lung problem. --- EXACERBATE (v, formal) = làm trầm trọng thêm một vấn đề đã tồn tại; collocation "exacerbate a condition/symptoms"; trái nghĩa "ameliorate/alleviate".

9. Rather than treating the body alone, this clinic takes a HOLISTIC WELL-BEING approach, considering a patient's sleep, diet and stress levels together. --- HOLISTIC WELL-BEING (noun phrase) = sức khỏe toàn diện, xem xét cả thể chất, tinh thần và xã hội; collocation "promote holistic well-being", "a holistic approach to health".

10. Rural doctors are still GRAPPLING WITH how to serve ageing patients with almost no extra funding or staff. --- GRAPPLE WITH (phrasal verb, academic) = vật lộn với một vấn đề khó khăn; luôn đi với giới từ "with" (grapple WITH an issue/challenge), gần nghĩa "wrestle with".

11. Once someone already has type-2 diabetes, treatment is largely CURATIVE, focusing on managing blood sugar rather than reversing the disease entirely. --- CURATIVE (adj) = mang tính chữa trị, tập trung vào bệnh đã có sẵn; collocation "a curative model/treatment"; trái nghĩa "preventive/preventative".

12. Vietnam's healthcare system is undergoing a PARADIGM SHIFT, moving away from simply treating sick patients and instead trying to stop people getting ill in the first place. --- PARADIGM SHIFT (noun phrase, academic) = sự thay đổi mô hình/tư duy căn bản; collocation "a paradigm shift in/from...to...", "undergo a paradigm shift".

passages.text: Until the late 1990s, the prevailing assumption in occupational medicine was that human beings are essentially flexible creatures, able to adapt to almost any working schedule provided they are given sufficient sleep. That view has since been largely overturned. A succession of carefully controlled laboratory studies, together with population data drawn from more than three hundred thousand European workers, suggests that an internal timing system — the circadian network of molecular clocks distributed throughout the body — exerts a far stronger influence on alertness, metabolism and mood than was previously acknowledged. Crucially, it differs from one individual to the next.
passages.title: Out of Phase

passages.text: The clearest articulation of this individual variation has come from Professor Till Roenneberg of Ludwig-Maximilian University in Munich. Working with what is now known as the Munich Chronotype Questionnaire, his team has classified hundreds of thousands of respondents along a continuous spectrum from extreme morning types, who feel alert before dawn, to extreme evening types, who do their best cognitive work after ten at night. Roenneberg argues that this distribution is genuinely biological, shaped substantially by the length of an individual's internal day, and that conventional workplace schedules systematically disadvantage those at the late end of the spectrum. He has coined the term social jet lag — the mismatch between an individual's biological clock and the clock imposed by employers and schools — and contends that this chronic misalignment, rather than total sleep duration alone, may explain a substantial portion of the long-term health costs traditionally attributed to shift work.
passages.title: Out of Phase

passages.text: Not every researcher accepts the strong version of this claim. Dr Frank Scheer, a chronobiologist at Harvard Medical School, agrees that misalignment matters but maintains that the absolute disruption of behavioural rhythms — eating, moving and sleeping at hours when the body expects rest — produces measurable metabolic damage independently of chronotype. In a series of controlled inpatient experiments, his group has shown that healthy volunteers asked to eat and sleep on a reversed schedule for ten days display elevated blood-glucose levels, raised blood pressure and altered patterns of fat storage, even when total calorie intake is held constant. Scheer concedes that evening types may suffer less acutely on night rosters, yet he insists that no chronotype is genuinely well suited to chronic nocturnal work; the metabolic penalty, in his reading, is universal.
passages.title: Out of Phase

passages.text: A third strand of research, led by Dr Céline Vetter at the University of Colorado, has attempted to test these competing models in the field rather than in the laboratory. Vetter's analyses of large nursing cohorts indicate that women whose chronotype aligns reasonably well with their assigned shift — late types on permanent nights, early types on permanent mornings — report fewer sleep complaints and slightly lower rates of cardiovascular disease over the long term than colleagues whose schedules pull against their natural timing. The effects, while statistically robust, are modest in magnitude, and Vetter is careful to emphasise that they do not amount to a clean bill of health for any form of night work. Rather, they suggest that the burden of misalignment can be reduced, though not eliminated, by attending to the underlying biology when rosters are designed.
passages.title: Out of Phase

passages.text: Practical reforms have begun to follow. Several Scandinavian hospitals have piloted what occupational physicians call chronotype-matched rostering, allowing nurses with documented late chronotypes to take a greater share of night duties in exchange for shorter day-shift commitments. Early evaluations suggest that staff turnover declines and reported fatigue falls, although the trials remain too small to draw firm conclusions about long-term illness rates. Critics, including the Swedish epidemiologist Professor Anders Knutsson, caution that workplace screening for chronotype risks creating a two-tier workforce in which workers identified as biologically unsuited to nights are quietly steered away from promotion, and that any policy framework must safeguard the right of individuals to decline such categorisation.
passages.title: Out of Phase

passages.text: The deeper scientific picture is also more complex than the early enthusiasm sometimes implied. Chronotype itself is not a fixed trait. It tends to drift later through adolescence, peak in late teenage years, and migrate earlier across middle and older age. Light exposure, meal timing and physical activity all modulate the underlying clock, which means that an apparently fixed evening type may shift towards a more moderate pattern when daily routines change. Roenneberg himself acknowledges that the questionnaire captures a snapshot, not a permanent identity, and that interventions targeting behavioural cues may prove as important as roster redesign.
passages.title: Out of Phase

passages.text: What appears to be emerging, then, is a more nuanced settlement. Few specialists now defend the older view that workers can simply train themselves to function on any schedule. At the same time, the strongest claims for chronotype-matching as a solution remain provisional. The most defensible position, on present evidence, is that circadian misalignment imposes real and measurable costs, that those costs vary across individuals in ways that biology can partly predict, and that humane scheduling will need to combine biological screening with environmental design and worker consent. The body clock, it seems, is neither an immovable obstacle nor a manageable inconvenience, but a system that workplaces ignore at considerable cost.

audio_scripts.text: Good morning. Today's lecture closes our chronobiology block — focusing on the clinical implications of circadian misalignment in shift-working healthcare staff. [pause:5s] The theoretical scaffolding I'll lean on comes from the work of Professor Sigrid Halvorsen — that's H-A-L-V-O-R-S-E-N, no umlaut on the O, no hyphen. Halvorsen's 2014 monograph reframed shift-induced fatigue from a simple sleep-debt model into what she calls "phase-delay vulnerability theory". [pause:3s] Firstly, a brief historical note. The longitudinal hospital cohort I'll refer to today was first recruited in 2002 — sorry, let me correct that, 2001; the published descriptive statistics in 2002 covered baseline measurements collected throughout 2001. So whenever I mention the baseline year for the Halvorsen cohort, please record 2001. [pause:3s] Right. A quick tense-orientation note, because the methodology has shifted noticeably across three decades. Circadian-misalignment research USED TO be conducted almost exclusively with wrist-actigraphy and self-reported sleep diaries; NOW the field combines actigraphy with salivary melatonin assays and continuous core-temperature telemetry; and from 2028 a multi-centre consortium WILL be deploying wearable cortisol patches as the primary biomarker. So past, present, future. For today's purposes I'm focusing on the CURRENT mixed-biomarker state — that is, melatonin plus temperature. [pause:3s] Moving to terminology. The phenomenon Halvorsen foregrounds — a sustained mismatch between an individual's internal biological clock and the externally imposed work schedule — is termed "phase-delay vulnerability". Now, you'll encounter related labels in the older literature: shift-lag, social jet lag, circadian disruption. These all gesture toward overlapping phenomena, but they are NOT interchangeable with Halvorsen's term. The currently accepted clinical term is phase-delay vulnerability — p-h-a-s-e-delay vulnerability. So when the older literature uses shift-lag or social jet lag, those are related but distinct constructs. [pause:3s] The next domain I want to address is what chronobiologists call the "alertness decrement profile". When investigators describe how reaction times degrade across a night shift, they sketch a graded profile running from minor lapses around two a.m. through micro-sleeps near four a.m. to gross attentional failures shortly before dawn. So, you know, you'LL see a junior doctor miss a decimal place on a drug-dose calculation at three a.m. — that's a micro-sleep failure. Or a nurse mis-reading a chart label just before handover — that's gross attentional failure. Now, these are illustrative cases, not the technical label itself. The umbrella term is the alertness decrement profile. [pause:3s] Now, the cohort data — and pay close attention here, because the quantifiers cluster densely. Of the four hundred and twenty nurses we sampled across six teaching hospitals last winter, MOST reported clinically significant fatigue on rotating-shift weeks — roughly sixty-eight per cent. Only a few — about eleven per cent — reported no measurable decrement, and some — twenty-one per cent — fell into an intermediate, context-dependent category. So fatigue dominates numerically, but the no-decrement tail, though small, is biomarker-interesting. [pause:3s] A second construct I want to flag is "chronotype mismatch". This refers to the gap between an individual's genetically anchored sleep-wake preference and the schedule the employer imposes. At Mercy Regional, our team logged ninety-four documented mismatch episodes across the cohort during one twelve-week rotation. [pause:3s] Crucially, the assumption that night-shift workers eventually adapt to inverted schedules is, frankly, not supported. Most of the nurses in our sample did NOT show the predicted monotonic improvement in alertness scores as weeks of consecutive night-shift exposure accumulated. Quite the opposite — many displayed a U-shaped curve, with a re-deterioration spike around weeks six to eight. So the older "adaptation hypothesis", which predicts linear habituation, is empirically NOT corroborated by our data. [pause:3s] Let me return to something I touched on earlier — the methodological tense-orientation point I made at the outset. That CURRENT mixed-biomarker state is what we're, sorta, gonna scrutinise in this afternoon's seminar. I want you to focus on the melatonin assay protocols specifically, not the future cortisol-patch deployment or the legacy actigraphy-only instruments. [pause:3s] To summarise: shift-induced fatigue is a phase-delay vulnerability, not a simple sleep debt; the technical term for biological-versus-schedule mismatch is phase-delay vulnerability; clinically significant fatigue dominates the cohort at roughly sixty-eight per cent; and the adaptation hypothesis is not empirically supported. Next week we'LL examine pharmacological countermeasures. Thank you. [pause:3s] (Q1) (Q2) (Q3) (Q4) (Q5) (Q6)

blocks.text: The three bar charts compare five countries — Japan, Sweden, the USA, Brazil and India — across three distinct health indicators in 2023: adult obesity prevalence, average life expectancy and the prevalence of common mental health disorders.

Overall, the United States stands out for the highest obesity rate and the heaviest mental-health burden, whereas Japan combines minimal obesity with the longest lifespans. A clear divide in longevity separates the high-income Asian and European nations from the remaining countries.

Regarding obesity, American adults recorded a striking 42%, roughly seven times the figure for India (6%) and tenfold that of Japan (4%). Brazil and Sweden occupied intermediate positions at 28% and 21% respectively. In terms of longevity, Japan led at 84 years, narrowly ahead of Sweden (83), while Brazil and India trailed at 76 and 70.

Concerning mental health, the US again topped the list at 21%, followed by Sweden at 17% and Brazil at 14%. India and Japan reported the lowest shares, at 11% and 8% respectively. The figures appear to track lifestyle pressures rather than national wealth alone.
The three bar charts compare adult obesity prevalence, average life expectancy and the prevalence of common mental health disorders across Japan, Sweden, the USA, Brazil and India in 2023.

Overall, the United States emerges as a striking outlier, recording both the highest obesity prevalence and the heaviest mental-health burden despite enjoying only middling longevity. Japan, by contrast, pairs negligible obesity with the greatest life expectancy, suggesting that national affluence translates unevenly into population health.

In terms of obesity, the American figure of 42% was arresting — fully tenfold Japan's 4% and roughly seven times India's 6%. Brazil and Sweden occupied the middle ground, at 28% and 21% respectively. The longevity ranking inverted this picture: Japan topped it at 84 years, fractionally ahead of Sweden's 83, whereas Brazil and India brought up the rear at 76 and 70.

As for mental health disorders, the United States again led at 21%, with Sweden close behind at 17% and Brazil registering 14%. India and Japan posted the slenderest shares, 11% and 8%. Notably, the affluent United States combined low life expectancy with elevated psychological distress, underscoring that prosperity is no guarantee of wellbeing.

blocks.text: The question of whether public health is best advanced through preventive medicine or through curative treatment continues to divide policymakers. While both pillars are necessary, I tend to side with those who consider prevention the more consequential investment.

On the one hand, those who defend curative care point out that no society can function without competent hospitals. It is in emergency rooms that trauma patients, stroke victims and people suffering acute infections are stabilised by intensive care teams, and many chronic illnesses such as diabetes simply cannot be reversed without long-term pharmacological management. What advocates of this view emphasise is the irreplaceable role of clinicians: if curative budgets were slashed, the most vulnerable groups would arguably be the first to suffer.

On the other hand, supporters of preventive medicine, including the WHO, argue that immunisation, regular screening and lifestyle counselling tend to deliver superior outcomes at a fraction of the cost. National vaccination programmes have eradicated diseases that once killed millions, while smoking-cessation campaigns are believed to have averted countless premature deaths. More importantly, by tackling risk factors before they escalate, prevention eases pressure on overstretched hospital wards.

In my view, although both approaches are complementary, prevention deserves the larger share of attention. Treatment is essentially reactive and addresses symptoms rather than root causes, whereas preventive policy targets the social and behavioural drivers of disease. Given the financial burden of ageing populations, governments that fail to invest upstream will find their healthcare systems financially unsustainable.

To conclude, although treatment must remain robustly funded for emergencies and chronic care, public health is more meaningfully improved when prevention is placed at the centre of policy. A balanced model, supported by epidemiological evidence, is the most sensible way forward.

Few debates in contemporary health policy are as enduring as that between proponents of preventive medicine and defenders of treatment-centred systems. Although both paradigms are indispensable, it is preventive intervention that, in my view, offers the most durable returns for public health and longevity.

Those who privilege curative care argue, not without justification, that no health system can dispense with sophisticated hospitals. What the trauma ward, the intensive care unit and the oncology clinic provide is irreplaceable: acute episodes demand immediate clinical action, and chronic conditions such as renal failure cannot be reversed through lifestyle modification alone. Were curative budgets drastically reduced, the burden would fall disproportionately on the elderly and the chronically ill.

Equally compelling, however, is the case for prevention. Drawing on decades of WHO epidemiological data and randomised controlled trial evidence, advocates contend that vaccination programmes, screening initiatives and behavioural counselling tend to avert disease at a fraction of the cost of late-stage intervention. So influential has this reasoning become that several OECD nations now channel a rising share of their budgets into upstream measures. Not only does this strategy ameliorate population-level outcomes; it also relieves the fiscal pressure exerted by ageing demographics.

In my considered view, while neither approach is a panacea, prevention deserves primacy. Treatment, however advanced, remains essentially reactive, addressing pathology only after it has manifested; prevention, by contrast, targets the upstream determinants — diet, sedentary behaviour, environmental exposure — that generate the bulk of disease burden. It is precisely this anticipatory logic that distinguishes a resilient health system from one condemned to a perpetual cycle of catching up.

To conclude, although curative services must remain robustly resourced, the most cost-effective and ethically defensible route to better public health runs through prevention. Integrating both, with prevention as the strategic anchor, is the policy posture best supported by current evidence.

Phần A

1. My grandfather has suffered from CHRONIC high blood pressure for over a decade. --- CHRONIC (adj) = mãn tính, kéo dài dai dẳng; collocation "a chronic illness/condition", "chronic pain"; đối lập với "acute" (cấp tính, xảy ra đột ngột).

2. People who already have heart problems are highly SUSCEPTIBLE to being badly affected by a bout of flu. --- SUSCEPTIBLE (adj) = dễ mắc, dễ bị ảnh hưởng; luôn đi với giới từ "to" (susceptible TO illness/infection), không dùng "with" hay "for".

3. Cutting down on salt and getting more sleep can gradually AMELIORATE high blood pressure. --- AMELIORATE (v, formal) = cải thiện một tình trạng vốn đã xấu; collocation "ameliorate symptoms/risk factors/a situation"; không dùng chung chung như "improve" (VD: không nói "ameliorate your English").

4. After breaking her hip, she spent three months undergoing REHABILITATION to relearn how to walk. --- REHABILITATION (n) = sự phục hồi chức năng sau chấn thương/bệnh tật; collocation "undergo rehabilitation", "a rehabilitation programme"; động từ liên quan "rehabilitate".

5. Better sanitation and access to clean water have quietly increased average human LONGEVITY. --- LONGEVITY (n, formal) = tuổi thọ, khái niệm trừu tượng về sự trường thọ; collocation "increased longevity", "human longevity"; phân biệt với "life expectancy" (chỉ số thống kê cụ thể).

6. Skipping breakfast every day and living on instant noodles is clearly DETRIMENTAL to a teenager's growth and concentration. --- DETRIMENTAL (adj, formal) = có hại, gây tổn hại; cấu trúc cố định "detrimental TO sth", không dùng "for"; trang trọng hơn "bad for".

7. A flu EPIDEMIC spread through three provinces last month, filling hospital wards within weeks. --- EPIDEMIC (n) = dịch bệnh lan rộng trong một khu vực/cộng đồng; collocation "a flu epidemic", "reach epidemic proportions"; khác "pandemic" (đại dịch lan ra toàn cầu).

8. Ignoring a mild cough for months can EXACERBATE a minor infection into a much more serious lung problem. --- EXACERBATE (v, formal) = làm trầm trọng thêm một vấn đề đã tồn tại; collocation "exacerbate a condition/symptoms"; trái nghĩa "ameliorate/alleviate".

9. Rather than treating the body alone, this clinic takes a HOLISTIC WELL-BEING approach, considering a patient's sleep, diet and stress levels together. --- HOLISTIC WELL-BEING (noun phrase) = sức khỏe toàn diện, xem xét cả thể chất, tinh thần và xã hội; collocation "promote holistic well-being", "a holistic approach to health".

10. Rural doctors are still GRAPPLING WITH how to serve ageing patients with almost no extra funding or staff. --- GRAPPLE WITH (phrasal verb, academic) = vật lộn với một vấn đề khó khăn; luôn đi với giới từ "with" (grapple WITH an issue/challenge), gần nghĩa "wrestle with".

11. Once someone already has type-2 diabetes, treatment is largely CURATIVE, focusing on managing blood sugar rather than reversing the disease entirely. --- CURATIVE (adj) = mang tính chữa trị, tập trung vào bệnh đã có sẵn; collocation "a curative model/treatment"; trái nghĩa "preventive/preventative".

12. Vietnam's healthcare system is undergoing a PARADIGM SHIFT, moving away from simply treating sick patients and instead trying to stop people getting ill in the first place. --- PARADIGM SHIFT (noun phrase, academic) = sự thay đổi mô hình/tư duy căn bản; collocation "a paradigm shift in/from...to...", "undergo a paradigm shift".
Phần B

1. Band 6: Sitting at a desk all day is not good for your back or your heart. - Band 7: A sedentary desk job can take a serious toll on both your posture and your cardiovascular health. - Band 8: Prolonged sedentary behaviour at a desk has been shown to compromise musculoskeletal alignment and cardiovascular function alike, irrespective of how active one is outside working hours.

2. Band 6: Many people still feel embarrassed to talk about depression or anxiety. - Band 7: A great deal of stigma still surrounds open conversations about depression or anxiety. - Band 8: Despite growing public awareness, a persistent stigma continues to discourage many from disclosing conditions such as depression or anxiety, even to close family members.

3. Band 6: Exercise cannot solve every health problem, but it does help a lot. - Band 7: While exercise is far from a panacea, it can meaningfully improve a wide range of health conditions. - Band 8: While exercise is hardly a panacea, the bulk of the evidence does seem to indicate that even modest physical activity can meaningfully ameliorate a host of chronic conditions.

4. Band 6: Doctors now think it is cheaper to stop illness before it happens than to treat it later. - Band 7: Medical professionals increasingly argue that preventive healthcare is more cost-effective than curative treatment. - Band 8: A growing consensus within the medical community holds that resources channelled into preventive healthcare yield far greater returns than those poured into curative treatment further down the line.

5. Band 6: Eating too much processed food can make people gain weight and feel tired. - Band 7: A diet dominated by processed food can contribute to weight gain and persistent fatigue. - Band 8: Diets dominated by ultra-processed food have been linked not merely to weight gain but to a subtler, more insidious fatigue that erodes day-to-day productivity.

6. Band 6: Someone's health is not only about their own choices; money and education matter too. - Band 7: A person's health is shaped by more than individual choices; income and education play a significant role as well. - Band 8: We must guard against attributing poor health purely to individual choice, since many conditions are, in essence, socially determined by factors such as income and educational attainment.

7. Band 6: Regular check-ups help doctors find diseases before they become serious. - Band 7: Routine check-ups allow doctors to detect diseases before they progress to a more serious stage. - Band 8: Routine screening enables clinicians to intervene at the earliest, most treatable stage of a disease, well before symptoms escalate into something considerably harder to manage.

8. Band 6: In the future, doctors might treat each patient differently based on their own body and genes. - Band 7: In the future, personalised medicine may allow doctors to tailor treatment to each patient's genetic profile. - Band 8: Within the next few decades, personalised medicine, informed by an individual's genetic profile, could well mark a paradigm shift away from the one-size-fits-all treatments of the past.

blocks.text: 1. Facts & Trends (Dữ liệu thực tế để support cho bài Writing)
Aging Population (Già hóa dân số): Increasing longevity means a higher proportion of elderly citizens, placing a massive financial strain on healthcare systems and pensions.
The Sedentary Epidemic: Desk jobs, screen time, and car-centric cities have drastically reduced daily physical exertion, leading to a surge in lifestyle-related diseases (Type 2 diabetes, obesity).
Mental Health Crisis: Workplace burnout and the psychological impact of social media are causing unprecedented rates of anxiety and depression among the youth.
Rising Healthcare Costs: Advanced medical technologies and expensive chronic disease management are making healthcare unaffordable for the average citizen in many countries.
2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: Who is responsible for public health? (Government vs. Individuals)
Government's Role: Can implement large-scale changes (sugar taxes, banning junk food ads); can build public infrastructure (parks, gyms); must provide affordable healthcare as a basic human right.
Individual's Role: Health is ultimately a personal choice; individuals control their daily diet, exercise routine, and sleep habits; relying solely on the government creates a dependent society.
Topic: Fast Food Tax (Should junk food be taxed highly?)
Pros: Discourages the consumption of unhealthy food (similar to tobacco taxes); generates revenue that can be reinvested into public health campaigns or subsidising healthy foods.

Cons: It is a "regressive tax" (disproportionately affects low-income families who rely on cheap food); violates individual freedom of choice; does not address the root cause of a sedentary lifestyle.
Topic: Modern vs. Traditional/Alternative Medicine
Modern Medicine Pros: Backed by rigorous empirical evidence and clinical trials; essential for treating acute illnesses, emergencies, and performing surgeries.
Alternative Medicine Pros: Often adopts a holistic approach; can be highly therapeutic for stress relief and chronic pain management; usually has fewer severe side effects.

Model answer (≈ 270 words)

The lifestyle overhaul I'd like to talk about is one I undertook in early 2024 — a fairly radical decision to cut ultra-processed food from my diet and commit to a non-negotiable 8,000-step walk every single day. Looking back, it was without doubt one of the more consequential choices I've made in my adult life.

What prompted the change was, frankly, a creeping sense of burnout. I'd been working punishing hours at a desk, surviving on instant noodles and energy drinks, and by late 2023 I was sleeping badly, gaining weight steadily, and feeling persistently foggy. The tipping point came when I read a Lancet review summarising the WHO's 2022 findings — namely, that diets dominated by ultra-processed food are causally linked to obesity, type-2 diabetes and a measurably shorter life expectancy. That genuinely shook me.

I won't pretend the transition was painless. The first three weeks were brutal, mainly because ultra-processed snacks are engineered for hyper-palatability — they hijack your reward system in a way that whole foods simply don't. What carried me through was a behavioural trick I'd picked up from atomic-habits literature: I stacked the new walk onto an existing routine, namely my morning coffee, which made it almost automatic within a fortnight.

The impact has, quite honestly, exceeded my expectations. I've shed roughly seven kilograms, but it's the cognitive uplift — sharper concentration, levelled mood, faster sleep onset — that has proved the most transformative. Were I to offer one takeaway, it would be this: meaningful change rarely requires a panacea. What it demands is consistency, evidence-based design, and a willingness to sit with discomfort until habit takes over.

Q1. Should governments regulate unhealthy food more strictly?
PEEL answer
Point: I'd argue regulation is not merely justified but, on balance, indispensable.

Evidence: The UK's Soft Drinks Industry Levy, introduced in 2018, was shown by Rogers et al. (BMC Medicine, 2023) to be associated with a 5,000-case-per-year reduction in childhood obesity admissions; meanwhile, the WHO's 2023 NCD report flagged that ultra-processed food now drives roughly 11 million premature deaths globally each year.
Explanation: What this suggests is that fiscal nudges work precisely because individual willpower is no match for products engineered for hyper-palatability.
Link: So while libertarians may baulk, the public-health calculus does seem to tilt firmly toward regulation.

On balance, I'd argue regulation is indispensable. The UK's 2018 sugar levy, according to Rogers and colleagues writing in BMC Medicine in 2023, correlated with around 5,000 fewer childhood obesity hospitalisations annually — a striking outcome for a relatively modest policy. The WHO's 2023 NCD report, meanwhile, attributes some 11 million premature deaths a year to ultra-processed diets. What this suggests is that personal willpower simply cannot compete with products engineered for hyper-palatability. So while libertarians push back, the public-health calculus does seem to tilt firmly toward state intervention.
Q2. Is mental health as important as physical health?
PEEL answer
Point: I would push back on the very framing — the two are not separable in any meaningful clinical sense.

Evidence: The Lancet Commission on Global Mental Health (Patel et al., 2018, updated 2023) estimated that mental disorders will cost the global economy USD 16 trillion by 2030; the WHO's 2022 World Mental Health Report further showed that depression is now the single largest contributor to non-fatal disease burden worldwide.

Explanation: Neuroimmunology research, particularly that of Dantzer (Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2018), has demonstrated that chronic stress measurably exacerbates inflammatory disease — so the mind-body divide is, frankly, a Cartesian fiction.
Link: Treating them as equivalent priorities is therefore not progressive politics; it's evidence-based medicine.

I'd actually push back on the framing — the two simply aren't separable in any clinically meaningful way. The Lancet Commission on Global Mental Health, updated in 2023, projected that psychiatric disorders will cost the world economy roughly USD 16 trillion by 2030, and the WHO's 2022 report identified depression as the leading cause of non-fatal disease burden globally. So treating mental and physical health as equivalent priorities isn't progressive politics — it's just evidence-based medicine.
Q3. Will personalised medicine become standard practice?
PEEL answer
Point: I'd cautiously predict that within the next two decades it will, though uneven access remains the elephant in the room.

Evidence: A Nature Medicine review by Ashley (2024) charted how pharmacogenomic testing has already cut adverse drug reactions by roughly 30% in early-adopter European hospitals; the OECD's 2023 Health at a Glance also flagged that genome-sequencing costs have collapsed from USD 100 million in 2001 to under USD 200 today.
Explanation: What this trajectory implies is that the technical barriers are essentially dissolving — what remains is largely a question of regulatory architecture and equitable distribution.
Link: So while standardisation seems all but inevitable for affluent systems, the global rollout will, I suspect, prove markedly more uneven.

1. Section Type

blocks.text: 3. Predict 3 Ideas (before listening)

She may link rising longevity to a financial burden on healthcare systems.

4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Good afternoon. Today I want to challenge a comfortable assumption: that biomedical advancements alone have driven the staggering rise in human longevity over the past century. They haven't — and the data is rather humbling.

> Let's start with the headline figure. Global life expectancy climbed from forty-seven years in 1950 to roughly seventy-three today. Now, the knee-jerk explanation is "better hospitals, better drugs." But careful epidemiological work — particularly McKeown's seminal analyses — attributes the lion's share of those gains not to pharmaceutical breakthroughs, but to sanitation, nutrition and housing. Penicillin, remarkable as it is, arrived after mortality had already plummeted.

> Here's the uncomfortable corollary. If medicine wasn't the panacea we imagined yesterday, it certainly isn't one today. Modern populations are increasingly susceptible to a cluster of so-called lifestyle diseases — type-two diabetes, cardiovascular pathology, certain cancers — all exacerbated by sedentary behaviour, ultra-processed diets and chronic psychological stress. You cannot, frankly, medicate your way out of a structural problem.

> Which brings us to the paradigm shift in public health: from curative to preventive medicine. The economics here are stark. Treating a stroke patient costs roughly fifteen times what it costs to ameliorate the upstream risk factors — blood pressure, glycaemic control, modest physical activity. A holistic approach, integrating mental health, sleep architecture and nutritional literacy, is no longer a wellness fad; it's fiscal common sense.

So, the next slide. Here is the finding that genuinely reframes the debate — the Whitehall studies, conducted by Michael Marmot and his team across the British civil service. Now, what makes Whitehall so instructive is that everyone in the sample had a stable job, the same national health system, the same broad access to care. And yet, mortality tracked rank with almost brutal precision. A clerk at the bottom of the hierarchy was roughly three times more likely to die prematurely than a permanent secretary at the top. Same hospitals, same drugs — radically different outcomes. The variable wasn't biology; it was, um, position in the social gradient. [pause]

What's doing the work here, Marmot argued, is autonomy — the degree of control one exercises over one's daily working life. Low control, high demand: that combination floods the body with cortisol, dysregulates blood pressure, suppresses immune function. So the stress isn't metaphorical; it is, if you like, etched into the cardiovascular system. This is why I'm wary of the wellness industry's relentless individualism — telling a zero-hours worker to practise mindfulness rather addresses the symptom while ignoring the wound. [pause]

A further consideration is the distribution of preventive gains. When public health campaigns succeed — smoking cessation is the textbook case — the affluent quit first and fastest, because they have the resources, the information, the supportive environment. The poor quit later, if at all. So a well-intentioned prevention drive can, paradoxically, widen the very inequalities it set out to close. Epidemiologists call this "intervention-generated inequality", and it's a sobering caveat. [pause]

So when we say longevity was a triumph of plumbing rather than pharmacology, the deeper truth is that it was, fundamentally, a triumph of equality. And that observation, frankly, leads us somewhere uncomfortable for the Treasury — let me flag the key policy implication…

> One caveat before we move on. Prevention places the burden of compliance on the individual, and we must guard against blaming patients for what are, in essence, socially determined conditions. Listen carefully now, because the next slide complicates that picture considerably…

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~286 words)

The question of whether public health is best advanced through preventive medicine or through curative treatment continues to divide policymakers. While both pillars are necessary, I tend to side with those who consider prevention the more consequential investment.

On the one hand, those who defend curative care point out that no society can function without competent hospitals. It is in emergency rooms that trauma patients, stroke victims and people suffering acute infections are stabilised by intensive care teams, and many chronic illnesses such as diabetes simply cannot be reversed without long-term pharmacological management. What advocates of this view emphasise is the irreplaceable role of clinicians: if curative budgets were slashed, the most vulnerable groups would arguably be the first to suffer.

On the other hand, supporters of preventive medicine, including the WHO, argue that immunisation, regular screening and lifestyle counselling tend to deliver superior outcomes at a fraction of the cost. National vaccination programmes have eradicated diseases that once killed millions, while smoking-cessation campaigns are believed to have averted countless premature deaths. More importantly, by tackling risk factors before they escalate, prevention eases pressure on overstretched hospital wards.

In my view, although both approaches are complementary, prevention deserves the larger share of attention. Treatment is essentially reactive and addresses symptoms rather than root causes, whereas preventive policy targets the social and behavioural drivers of disease. Given the financial burden of ageing populations, governments that fail to invest upstream will find their healthcare systems financially unsustainable.

To conclude, although treatment must remain robustly funded for emergencies and chronic care, public health is more meaningfully improved when prevention is placed at the centre of policy. A balanced model, supported by epidemiological evidence, is the most sensible way forward.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~305 words)

Few debates in contemporary health policy are as enduring as that between proponents of preventive medicine and defenders of treatment-centred systems. Although both paradigms are indispensable, it is preventive intervention that, in my view, offers the most durable returns for public health and longevity.

Those who privilege curative care argue, not without justification, that no health system can dispense with sophisticated hospitals. What the trauma ward, the intensive care unit and the oncology clinic provide is irreplaceable: acute episodes demand immediate clinical action, and chronic conditions such as renal failure cannot be reversed through lifestyle modification alone. Were curative budgets drastically reduced, the burden would fall disproportionately on the elderly and the chronically ill.

Equally compelling, however, is the case for prevention. Drawing on decades of WHO epidemiological data and randomised controlled trial evidence, advocates contend that vaccination programmes, screening initiatives and behavioural counselling tend to avert disease at a fraction of the cost of late-stage intervention. So influential has this reasoning become that several OECD nations now channel a rising share of their budgets into upstream measures. Not only does this strategy ameliorate population-level outcomes; it also relieves the fiscal pressure exerted by ageing demographics.

In my considered view, while neither approach is a panacea, prevention deserves primacy. Treatment, however advanced, remains essentially reactive, addressing pathology only after it has manifested; prevention, by contrast, targets the upstream determinants — diet, sedentary behaviour, environmental exposure — that generate the bulk of disease burden. It is precisely this anticipatory logic that distinguishes a resilient health system from one condemned to a perpetual cycle of catching up.

To conclude, although curative services must remain robustly resourced, the most cost-effective and ethically defensible route to better public health runs through prevention. Integrating both, with prevention as the strategic anchor, is the policy posture best supported by current evidence.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 dùng cấu trúc phức cao cấp xuyên suốt (inversion 'So influential has this reasoning become', cleft 'What the trauma ward... provides is irreplaceable', đảo ngữ điều kiện 'Were curative budgets reduced') trong khi Band 7 chỉ dùng một vài lần.
•  Band 8 dẫn bằng chứng cụ thể hơn (WHO + RCT + OECD spending shifts) và nominalisation dày đặc ('upstream determinants', 'anticipatory logic'), nâng Task Response và Lexical Resource lên một bậc.

•  Band 8 có cohesion liền mạch với connector tinh tế ('Equally compelling, however', 'Not only does this... it also', 'by contrast') và register học thuật nhất quán, không còn cụm hơi đời thường như 'kept alive' của bản 7.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Ít vận động, tĩnh tại — lối sống hoặc công việc ít hoạt động thể chất.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> A **sedentary** office routine left me chronically fatigued and increasingly susceptible to minor ailments.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Liên tưởng 'sit' (ngồi) ẩn trong gốc Latin 'sedere' → sedentary = ngồi nhiều, ít vận động.
vocabulary.common_error: Không dùng *sedentary* như đồng nghĩa với *lazy*; từ này mô tả lối sống/công việc ít vận động.
vocabulary.definition_en: (of a lifestyle, job or person) involving or characterised by much sitting and little physical activity
vocabulary.definition_vi: ít vận động, tĩnh tại (lối sống, công việc)
vocabulary.example: A sedentary office routine left me chronically fatigued and increasingly susceptible to minor ailments.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Liên tưởng 'sit' (ngồi) ẩn trong gốc Latin 'sedere' → sedentary = ngồi nhiều, ít vận động.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tuổi thọ, sự trường thọ — thời gian sống dài.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Advancements in medical science have significantly increased average human **longevity** globally.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
long (dài) + -evity (liên quan 'aevum' = thời gian sống) → sống dài → tuổi thọ.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'longevity' (tuổi thọ nói chung, danh từ trừu tượng) với 'life expectancy' (tuổi thọ kỳ vọng, một số liệu thống kê cụ thể).
vocabulary.definition_en: long life, or the length of time that a person or thing lives or lasts
vocabulary.definition_vi: tuổi thọ, sự trường thọ
vocabulary.example: Advancements in medical science have significantly increased average human longevity globally.
vocabulary.memory_hook: long (dài) + -evity (liên quan 'aevum' = thời gian sống) → sống dài → tuổi thọ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thuốc chữa bách bệnh, giải pháp vạn năng — thường mang nghĩa hoài nghi vì không thực sự tồn tại.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> While exercise is hardly a **panacea**, the bulk of peer-reviewed evidence does seem to indicate that even modest activity can meaningfully ameliorate metabolic risk.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Pan- (toàn bộ, như 'pandemic') + -acea (chữa bệnh) → thuốc chữa được TẤT CẢ bệnh.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Panacea' luôn mang hàm ý phóng đại/hoài nghi — thường xuất hiện trong cụm phủ định 'no panacea' hay 'hardly a panacea', hiếm khi dùng để khen thật.
vocabulary.definition_en: a supposed remedy or solution that is claimed to cure all diseases or solve all problems
vocabulary.definition_vi: thuốc chữa bách bệnh, giải pháp vạn năng (thường mang nghĩa hoài nghi)
vocabulary.example: While exercise is hardly a panacea, the bulk of peer-reviewed evidence does seem to indicate that even modest activity can meaningfully ameliorate metabolic risk.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Pan- (toàn bộ, như 'pandemic') + -acea (chữa bệnh) → thuốc chữa được TẤT CẢ bệnh.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Dễ mắc, dễ bị ảnh hưởng bởi một bệnh hoặc tình trạng nào đó.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Modern populations are increasingly **susceptible** to a cluster of so-called lifestyle diseases.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
sus- (dưới) + -cept (nắm bắt, take) → dễ 'bị nắm bắt' bởi bệnh → dễ mắc.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Susceptible' đi với giới từ 'to', không phải 'with' hay 'for': susceptible TO illness.
vocabulary.definition_en: highly likely to be affected by, influenced by, or to contract a particular disease or condition
vocabulary.definition_vi: dễ mắc, dễ bị ảnh hưởng bởi (bệnh tật, tác động)
vocabulary.example: Modern populations are increasingly susceptible to a cluster of so-called lifestyle diseases.
vocabulary.memory_hook: sus- (dưới) + -cept (nắm bắt, take) → dễ 'bị nắm bắt' bởi bệnh → dễ mắc.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Cải thiện, làm cho một tình huống xấu trở nên tốt hơn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Treating a stroke patient costs roughly fifteen times what it costs to **ameliorate** the upstream risk factors.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc Latin 'melior' (tốt hơn, như comparative 'better') → a-melior-ate → làm cho tốt hơn.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Ameliorate' là động từ trang trọng, chỉ dùng cho việc cải thiện một tình trạng đã XẤU sẵn, không dùng chung chung như 'improve' (VD: không nói 'ameliorate your English skills').
vocabulary.definition_en: to make a bad or unsatisfactory situation better; to improve
vocabulary.definition_vi: cải thiện, làm cho (tình huống xấu) tốt hơn
vocabulary.example: Treating a stroke patient costs roughly fifteen times what it costs to ameliorate the upstream risk factors.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Gốc Latin 'melior' (tốt hơn, như comparative 'better') → a-melior-ate → làm cho tốt hơn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự phục hồi chức năng sau bệnh tật, chấn thương hoặc nghiện.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> After the car crash, she had to undergo months of **rehabilitation** to regain her mobility.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
re- (lại) + habilis (có khả năng, như 'able') → làm cho 'có khả năng' trở lại → phục hồi.
vocabulary.common_error: Nói *undergo rehabilitation* hoặc *a rehabilitation programme*; không dùng *do rehabilitation* trong văn trang trọng.
vocabulary.definition_en: the process of restoring a person to health, normal life, or functioning after illness, injury or addiction
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự phục hồi chức năng (sau bệnh tật, chấn thương hoặc nghiện)
vocabulary.example: After the car crash, she had to undergo months of rehabilitation to regain her mobility.
vocabulary.memory_hook: re- (lại) + habilis (có khả năng, như 'able') → làm cho 'có khả năng' trở lại → phục hồi.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự kỳ thị, định kiến xã hội gắn với một tình trạng hoặc đặc điểm nào đó.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> There is unfortunately still a lot of **stigma** attached to seeking help for depression.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc Hy Lạp 'stigma' = vết sẹo do đóng dấu nô lệ/tội phạm → nghĩa hiện đại: vết nhơ xã hội, sự kỳ thị.
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng *a stigma attached to something* hoặc *stigma surrounding something*; không nói *stigma for doing* một cách máy móc.
vocabulary.definition_en: a mark of social disgrace or shame strongly associated with a particular circumstance, quality, or person
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự kỳ thị, định kiến xã hội (gắn với một tình trạng cụ thể)
vocabulary.example: There is unfortunately still a lot of stigma attached to seeking help for depression.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Gốc Hy Lạp 'stigma' = vết sẹo do đóng dấu nô lệ/tội phạm → nghĩa hiện đại: vết nhơ xã hội, sự kỳ thị.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Mãn tính, kéo dài dai dẳng — thường dùng để mô tả bệnh tật.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Patients who are **chronically** ill require long-term care and financial support.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc Hy Lạp 'chronos' (thời gian, như 'chronology') → chronic = kéo dài theo thời gian → mãn tính.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Chronic' (mãn tính, kéo dài) khác với 'acute' (cấp tính, xảy ra đột ngột và nghiêm trọng) — hai từ này thường bị lẫn lộn.
vocabulary.definition_en: (of an illness) persisting for a long time or constantly recurring; long-lasting and difficult to eradicate
vocabulary.definition_vi: mãn tính, kéo dài dai dẳng (bệnh tật)
vocabulary.example: Patients who are chronically ill require long-term care and financial support.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Gốc Hy Lạp 'chronos' (thời gian, như 'chronology') → chronic = kéo dài theo thời gian → mãn tính.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sức khoẻ toàn diện, xem xét cả thể chất, tinh thần và xã hội thay vì chỉ chữa triệu chứng riêng lẻ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> A **holistic** approach, integrating mental health, sleep architecture and nutritional literacy, is no longer a wellness fad; it is fiscal common sense.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Holistic' từ 'whole' (toàn bộ) → nhìn con người như một tổng thể, không tách rời thể chất và tinh thần.
vocabulary.common_error: Không viết *wellbeing* và *well-being* lẫn lộn trong cùng bài; chọn một chuẩn, ưu tiên *well-being* theo bộ thẻ này.
vocabulary.definition_en: a state of health that takes into account the whole person — physical, mental and social — rather than treating symptoms in isolation
vocabulary.definition_vi: sức khoẻ toàn diện (cả thể chất, tinh thần và xã hội)
vocabulary.example: A holistic approach, integrating mental health, sleep architecture and nutritional literacy, is no longer a wellness fad; it is fiscal common sense.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Holistic' từ 'whole' (toàn bộ) → nhìn con người như một tổng thể, không tách rời thể chất và tinh thần.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Phòng ngừa, mang tính ngăn chặn trước khi vấn đề xảy ra.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Doctors and health experts are now heavily emphasising **preventive** measures, such as proper nutrition and regular physical activity, to improve overall well-being before a crisis hits.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
pre- (trước) + vent (đến, như 'venir') → 'đến trước' vấn đề để chặn nó lại → phòng ngừa.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Preventive' và 'preventative' đều đúng và cùng nghĩa, nhưng 'preventive' được xem là dạng ưa dùng hơn trong văn phong học thuật/IELTS.
vocabulary.definition_en: designed to stop something (especially disease) from happening before it starts
vocabulary.definition_vi: phòng ngừa, ngăn chặn trước
vocabulary.example: Doctors and health experts are now heavily emphasising preventive measures, such as proper nutrition and regular physical activity, to improve overall well-being before a crisis hits.
vocabulary.memory_hook: pre- (trước) + vent (đến, như 'venir') → 'đến trước' vấn đề để chặn nó lại → phòng ngừa.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Dịch bệnh hoặc hiện tượng tiêu cực lan rộng trong một cộng đồng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Desk jobs, screen time, and car-centric cities have drastically reduced daily physical exertion, leading to a surge in an obesity **epidemic**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
epi- (trên, giữa) + demos (dân chúng, như 'democracy') → thứ lan 'giữa dân chúng' → dịch bệnh.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Epidemic' (dịch bệnh trong một khu vực/cộng đồng) khác 'pandemic' (đại dịch lan ra toàn cầu) về quy mô.
vocabulary.definition_en: a widespread occurrence of an infectious disease, or of an undesirable phenomenon, within a community at a particular time
vocabulary.definition_vi: dịch bệnh, hiện tượng lan rộng (nghĩa bóng: tình trạng phổ biến đáng lo ngại)
vocabulary.example: Desk jobs, screen time, and car-centric cities have drastically reduced daily physical exertion, leading to a surge in an obesity epidemic.
vocabulary.memory_hook: epi- (trên, giữa) + demos (dân chúng, như 'democracy') → thứ lan 'giữa dân chúng' → dịch bệnh.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Có hại, gây tổn hại tới sức khoẻ hoặc tình trạng nào đó.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> I made a conscious decision to cut out fast food after realising how **detrimental** it was to my well-being.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Detriment' (thiệt hại) + -al → detrimental = gây thiệt hại, có hại.
vocabulary.common_error: Giới từ cố định là *detrimental to*, không phải *detrimental for*; tránh lặp *detrimental harm* vì thừa nghĩa.
vocabulary.definition_en: tending to cause harm or damage; harmful
vocabulary.definition_vi: có hại, gây tổn hại
vocabulary.example: I made a conscious decision to cut out fast food after realising how detrimental it was to my well-being.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Detriment' (thiệt hại) + -al → detrimental = gây thiệt hại, có hại.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự kiên cường tinh thần, khả năng phục hồi tâm lý sau căng thẳng hoặc nghịch cảnh.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Workplace burnout and the psychological impact of social media have made it more important than ever to build **mental resilience** among young people.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Resilience' như một quả bóng cao su bật lại sau va đập → khả năng phục hồi tinh thần sau khó khăn.
vocabulary.common_error: Thường nói *build/develop mental resilience*; không dùng *a mental resilience* vì đây thường là danh từ không đếm được.
vocabulary.definition_en: the capacity to recover quickly from psychological difficulties and adapt well in the face of stress or adversity
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự kiên cường tinh thần, khả năng phục hồi tâm lý
vocabulary.example: Workplace burnout and the psychological impact of social media have made it more important than ever to build mental resilience among young people.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Resilience' như một quả bóng cao su bật lại sau va đập → khả năng phục hồi tinh thần sau khó khăn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Làm trầm trọng thêm, làm xấu đi một tình trạng vốn đã tiêu cực.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Consuming highly processed foods and experiencing chronic stress can severely **exacerbate** these conditions, making individuals even more susceptible to infectious diseases.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
ex- (ra ngoài, mạnh) + acerbus (chua gắt, cay đắng) → làm mọi thứ 'gắt' hơn → trầm trọng thêm.
vocabulary.common_error: *Exacerbate* đã có nghĩa “làm tệ hơn”; không viết *exacerbate worse* và chỉ dùng với vấn đề/tình trạng tiêu cực.
vocabulary.definition_en: to make a problem, bad situation, or negative feeling worse
vocabulary.definition_vi: làm trầm trọng thêm, làm xấu đi (một vấn đề đã tệ sẵn)
vocabulary.example: Consuming highly processed foods and experiencing chronic stress can severely exacerbate these conditions, making individuals even more susceptible to infectious diseases.
vocabulary.memory_hook: ex- (ra ngoài, mạnh) + acerbus (chua gắt, cay đắng) → làm mọi thứ 'gắt' hơn → trầm trọng thêm.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chứng béo phì — tình trạng thừa cân nghiêm trọng, gây nguy cơ cho sức khoẻ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The modern sedentary lifestyle has led to a significant rise in various ailments, most notably **obesity** and cardiovascular diseases.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Obese' nghe gần 'over-eat' (ăn quá nhiều) → obesity = tình trạng béo phì do ăn/tích mỡ quá mức.
vocabulary.common_error: *Obesity* là danh từ không đếm được; không nói *an obesity* hoặc *obesities* khi nói về tình trạng sức khỏe.
vocabulary.definition_en: the condition of being seriously overweight, typically to a degree that poses a risk to health
vocabulary.definition_vi: chứng béo phì
vocabulary.example: The modern sedentary lifestyle has led to a significant rise in various ailments, most notably obesity and cardiovascular diseases.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Obese' nghe gần 'over-eat' (ăn quá nhiều) → obesity = tình trạng béo phì do ăn/tích mỡ quá mức.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vật lộn với, cố gắng giải quyết một vấn đề hoặc thách thức khó khăn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The issue of rising healthcare costs has come under intense scrutiny, as experts **grapple with** how to fund an ageing population, often at the expense of other public services.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Grapple' nguyên nghĩa là 'vật lộn tay đôi' (như đấu vật) → nghĩa bóng: vật lộn với một vấn đề khó.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn dùng *grapple with + problem/issue*; không dùng *grapple to* và tránh dùng cho nhiệm vụ quá đơn giản.
vocabulary.definition_en: to try to deal with or understand a difficult problem or challenge
vocabulary.definition_vi: vật lộn với, cố gắng giải quyết (một vấn đề khó khăn)
vocabulary.example: The issue of rising healthcare costs has come under intense scrutiny, as experts grapple with how to fund an ageing population, often at the expense of other public services.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Grapple' nguyên nghĩa là 'vật lộn tay đôi' (như đấu vật) → nghĩa bóng: vật lộn với một vấn đề khó.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Được chứng nhận là hoàn toàn khoẻ mạnh sau khi kiểm tra.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The doctor examined him thoroughly and gave him a **clean bill of health**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Tưởng tượng bác sĩ ký vào 'bill' (hoá đơn/giấy) ghi 'sạch' (clean) = không bệnh tật gì → được chứng nhận khoẻ mạnh.
collocations: give someone a clean bill of health
receive a clean bill of health
vocabulary.common_error: Cụm cố định là *give/receive a clean bill of health*; không thay *clean* bằng *good*.
vocabulary.definition_en: an official statement or judgement that someone or something is in good health or good condition
vocabulary.definition_vi: giấy chứng nhận sức khoẻ tốt, được xác nhận là hoàn toàn khoẻ mạnh
vocabulary.example: The doctor examined him thoroughly and gave him a clean bill of health.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Tưởng tượng bác sĩ ký vào 'bill' (hoá đơn/giấy) ghi 'sạch' (clean) = không bệnh tật gì → được chứng nhận khoẻ mạnh.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Đang hồi phục, đang khá dần lên sau một trận ốm hoặc chấn thương.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> She had a severe flu last week, but thankfully she is **on the mend** now.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Mend' = vá lại, sửa chữa (như mend a shirt) → cơ thể đang được 'vá lành' → đang hồi phục.
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng với động từ *be*: *is on the mend*; đây là cách nói thân mật, không phù hợp báo cáo y khoa chính thức.
vocabulary.definition_en: recovering from an illness or injury; getting better
vocabulary.definition_vi: đang hồi phục, đang khá dần lên (sau bệnh/chấn thương)
vocabulary.example: She had a severe flu last week, but thankfully she is on the mend now.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Mend' = vá lại, sửa chữa (như mend a shirt) → cơ thể đang được 'vá lành' → đang hồi phục.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Từ bỏ một thói quen xấu, đặc biệt là hút thuốc hoặc nghiện chất kích thích.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> It takes a lot of willpower and support to **kick the habit** of smoking.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Kick' như đá văng thứ gì đó ra khỏi cuộc sống → kick the habit = đá bay thói quen xấu, từ bỏ nó.
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng *kick the habit* hoặc *kick the habit of smoking*; không nói *kick a habit* khi muốn dùng đúng thành ngữ cố định.
vocabulary.definition_en: to succeed in stopping doing something harmful that has become a regular practice, especially smoking or drug use
vocabulary.definition_vi: từ bỏ (một thói quen xấu, thường là hút thuốc/nghiện)
vocabulary.example: It takes a lot of willpower and support to kick the habit of smoking.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Kick' như đá văng thứ gì đó ra khỏi cuộc sống → kick the habit = đá bay thói quen xấu, từ bỏ nó.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tuổi thọ trung bình kỳ vọng, một chỉ số thống kê phổ biến trong Writing Task 1.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Advancements in medical science have significantly increased average **life expectancy** globally.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
life (đời sống) + expectancy (điều được kỳ vọng, như 'expect') → số năm sống được kỳ vọng.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Life expectancy' là một chỉ số thống kê cụ thể (VD: 84 years), khác với 'longevity' vốn là khái niệm trừu tượng hơn về tuổi thọ dài.
vocabulary.definition_en: the average number of years a person is expected to live, based on statistical data for a given population
vocabulary.definition_vi: tuổi thọ trung bình (kỳ vọng), thường dùng trong số liệu thống kê dân số
vocabulary.example: Advancements in medical science have significantly increased average life expectancy globally.
vocabulary.memory_hook: life (đời sống) + expectancy (điều được kỳ vọng, như 'expect') → số năm sống được kỳ vọng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hệ miễn dịch — mạng lưới tế bào và cơ quan giúp cơ thể chống lại bệnh tật.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Eating plenty of fruits and vegetables helps to boost your **immune system**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Immune' = miễn nhiễm (không bị ảnh hưởng) → immune system = hệ thống giúp cơ thể miễn nhiễm với bệnh tật.
vocabulary.common_error: Không dùng *immunity system*; cụm chuẩn là *immune system*, còn *immunity* là khả năng miễn dịch.
vocabulary.definition_en: the network of cells, tissues and organs in the body that work together to defend it against infections and disease
vocabulary.definition_vi: hệ miễn dịch
vocabulary.example: Eating plenty of fruits and vegetables helps to boost your immune system.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Immune' = miễn nhiễm (không bị ảnh hưởng) → immune system = hệ thống giúp cơ thể miễn nhiễm với bệnh tật.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự thay đổi mô hình hoặc tư duy căn bản trong một lĩnh vực hay cách tiếp cận.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Which brings us to the **paradigm shift** in public health: from curative to preventive medicine.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Paradigm' = khuôn mẫu tư duy chung của cả cộng đồng; 'shift' = dịch chuyển → cả khuôn mẫu tư duy thay đổi hẳn.
vocabulary.common_error: Chỉ dùng *paradigm shift* cho thay đổi nền tảng về mô hình/cách nghĩ, không phóng đại một điều chỉnh nhỏ.
vocabulary.definition_en: a fundamental change in the basic assumptions or approach underlying a theory, field, or practice
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự thay đổi mô hình/tư duy căn bản, bước ngoặt trong cách tiếp cận
vocabulary.example: Which brings us to the paradigm shift in public health: from curative to preventive medicine.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Paradigm' = khuôn mẫu tư duy chung của cả cộng đồng; 'shift' = dịch chuyển → cả khuôn mẫu tư duy thay đổi hẳn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Mang tính chữa trị, tập trung điều trị bệnh đã xảy ra thay vì phòng ngừa.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The economics here are stark: it is far cheaper to shift from a **curative** model to a preventive one.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Cure' (chữa khỏi) + -ative → curative = có tính chữa trị, tập trung vào bệnh đã có sẵn.
vocabulary.common_error: Không nhầm *curative* (có tính chữa trị) với *curable* (có thể chữa khỏi); thường đi với *treatment, medicine, model*.
vocabulary.definition_en: relating to or able to cure disease; focused on treating an illness that already exists rather than preventing it
vocabulary.definition_vi: mang tính chữa trị, điều trị (bệnh đã xảy ra), đối lập với phòng ngừa
vocabulary.example: The economics here are stark: it is far cheaper to shift from a curative model to a preventive one.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Cure' (chữa khỏi) + -ative → curative = có tính chữa trị, tập trung vào bệnh đã có sẵn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Được hình thành chủ yếu bởi các yếu tố xã hội như thu nhập, giáo dục, điều kiện làm việc, chứ không chỉ do lựa chọn cá nhân.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> We must guard against blaming patients for what are, in essence, **socially determined** conditions.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Socially' (bởi xã hội) + 'determined' (được quyết định) → sức khoẻ không chỉ do cá nhân mà còn do hoàn cảnh xã hội quyết định.
vocabulary.common_error: Không dùng *social determined*; cần trạng từ *socially* bổ nghĩa cho phân từ *determined*.
vocabulary.definition_en: shaped or caused primarily by social factors (such as income, education, or working conditions) rather than by individual choice or biology alone
vocabulary.definition_vi: do yếu tố xã hội quyết định (thu nhập, giáo dục, điều kiện làm việc...), không chỉ do lựa chọn cá nhân
vocabulary.example: We must guard against blaming patients for what are, in essence, socially determined conditions.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Socially' (bởi xã hội) + 'determined' (được quyết định) → sức khoẻ không chỉ do cá nhân mà còn do hoàn cảnh xã hội quyết định.
